archetype.name: Gunslinger (pocket-bound)
archetype.definition: A statue-still pocket passer who has always pushed the ball into tight windows. He lives on intermediate and deep throws from a clean pocket, gives almost nothing as a runner, and has accepted a higher interception count as the price of the aggression for 18 years.

report.headline: Volume is there, the deep ball isn't: a 6-6 start that should correct
report.take:
Stafford is coming off the best season of his late career: an NFL-high 46 touchdowns, 0.228 EPA per play (8th) and a 53.3% success rate (6th). Through four games of 2026 he looks like a different passer on paper: 0.08 EPA per dropback (21st of 42), six interceptions against six touchdowns, and a CPOE that ranks 29th. The process underneath has not collapsed, though. His aggressiveness (18.5%) and intended air yards (9.6) almost match last year's 19.3% and 9.2 aDOT. His time to throw (2.79) is identical. He is being pressured on only 14.4% of dropbacks, 3rd-fewest in the league. This is the same quarterback running the same plan. What has changed is what happens when the ball goes long.

The season splits cleanly by depth. Between 10 and 19 air yards he has been excellent: 0.427 EPA per attempt and a 59% success rate on 39 throws. That is where the Davante Adams connection lives, with Adams drawing 38 targets at 0.393 EPA each. Beyond 20 yards he is 6-of-21 with three interceptions and a -6.4 CPOE. Underneath, 86 short attempts at 72% completion have produced almost nothing (0.018 EPA), and Kyren Williams' 25 targets at 0.037 EPA say the checkdown game is just treading water. Puka Nacua, second among wideouts with 21 targets, is at 0.053 EPA per target. The offense is leaning on one receiver and one depth band.

The numbers hide two things. First, the interceptions are clustered rather than spread out. Five of the six came in one-score game states, and three came on just 21 deep balls. His bad-throw rate (10.5%) is actually lower than any charted season in his career; he has never been below 16%. That points to bad luck and a few forced shots, not erratic accuracy. Second, the yardage total (4th in the league) is mostly volume. The 390- and 317-yard games came on 55 and 51 attempts, with passing EPA of -0.7 and +1.1. Week 1 against San Francisco is the real outlier and also the clearest warning. When he was pressured on 28% of dropbacks, a quarter of his throws were charted as bad and he managed 155 yards.

He is 38 with a top-four defense behind him and a coach who throws more than the situation predicts (6th in pass rate over expected). The structure for a rebound is in place. Deep accuracy at 28.6% on a 21-throw sample should drift back toward his norm, and the interception rate (3.7%) sits well above last year's pace of eight in 17 games. The open question is whether age has shaved anything off the deep ball. Four games can't answer that, but the next few against weaker defenses will tell a lot.

strengths.title: Intermediate game carrying the offense
strengths.body: His 10-19 yard throws produce 0.427 EPA per attempt with a 59% success rate. That is the most efficient band of the field for him by a wide margin, and it is built largely around Adams. The skill is long-standing, consistent with years of 19-23% aggressiveness. It should hold as long as the protection does.

strengths.title: Clean pockets, few sacks
strengths.body: He is pressured on only 14.4% of dropbacks (3rd) and sacked on 3.6% (7th). His pressure-to-sack rate of 20.8% tracks with last year's 19.7%, which ranked 9th. Quick processing and a line keeping him upright let him stay patient in the pocket, and that is what feeds the intermediate game.

strengths.title: Up-tempo and lead-protecting efficiency
strengths.body: In no-huddle he has 0.387 EPA and an 11.7 CPOE on 29 plays. Playing with a lead of nine or more he is at 0.239 EPA. Both are small samples, but they suggest the offense is at its best when the tempo is up or the defense has given him a cushion. With the defense at 4th in EPA allowed, he should get more of those leads.

concerns.title: Deep ball has gone cold
concerns.body: He is 6-of-21 on throws of 20+ air yards with three interceptions and -0.109 EPA. Half of his picks came on fewer than 13% of his attempts. The volume of shots is normal for him, so this is execution or luck rather than scheme. At 38, a real loss of arm strength can't be ruled out after only 21 throws, but the sample is too thin to call it.

concerns.title: Turnovers in close games
concerns.body: Five of his six interceptions came with the score within one possession, where his EPA is -0.023. Some turnover volume is simply who he is: his interception totals have ranked in the bottom third most seasons of his career. Still, a 3.7% interception rate is above his recent norm and should come down.

concerns.title: Third downs and empty short game
concerns.body: He faces an average of 8.5 yards to go on third down and converts 38.5%, at -0.22 EPA. That is partly because early-down throws underneath gain so little: 86 short attempts add just 0.018 EPA. The fix is on early downs more than on third down.

trend.note: His passing EPA by week went -5.6 vs SF, +18.6 vs NYG, -0.7 at DEN and +1.1 at PHI. The last two games brought 51-plus attempts and 300-plus yards each, but almost no efficiency and four interceptions between them.

nextGame.headline: Leaky Buffalo secondary, without Benford, sets up a rebound
nextGame.body:
Buffalo's defense ranks 29th in EPA, 28th against the pass and 27th in explosive pass rate allowed. It gives up 21.3 PPR points, 297 yards and 2.5 touchdowns a game to quarterbacks, all among the five worst marks in the league. That fits Stafford's intermediate strength, and a soft secondary is the best possible test of whether his deep misses are noise. The one real threat is the rush: Buffalo hits the quarterback at the 5th-highest rate. His two worst games came when he was pressured on 25-28% of dropbacks. The game is in a dome, the Rams are 2.5-point home favorites, and Buffalo's offense ranks 3rd in EPA, so he may need to keep scoring.

On Buffalo's side, top corner Christian Benford (91% of snaps) is out. Slot corner Dee Alford and Te'Cory Couch are questionable, which could leave the secondary very thin. Interior linemen T.J. Sanders (out) and Ed Oliver (questionable) weaken the middle of that pass rush. For the Rams, tight end Colby Parkinson (64% of snaps) is listed out with an estimated return of game day, and Terrance Ferguson is on IR. That pushes the tight end work onto Tyler Higbee and probably more three-receiver looks. Konata Mumpfield, the third receiver, is questionable with a shoulder bruise, which could narrow the passing tree to Adams and Nacua even further.

keyMatchups.title: Adams vs. Benford-less corners
keyMatchups.body: Adams has been the only consistently efficient target (0.393 EPA on 38 targets). Buffalo loses its every-down corner and may also be missing slot help. Expect Adams' target share to stay heavy and his yards per target to climb.

keyMatchups.title: Buffalo's hit rate vs. clean pocket
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo gets hits on 19.8% of dropbacks (5th), while Stafford has been pressured just 14.4% of the time. His floor depends on which side wins: at 25-28% pressure he went 155 yards vs SF and threw two picks at DEN. With Oliver questionable and Sanders out, the Buffalo interior is thinner than its season rate suggests.

keyMatchups.title: Explosive shots against a soft back end
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo allows explosive passes at the 27th-worst rate, and its deep EPA allowed is only middling (14th). This is the best chance yet for his 28.6% deep completion rate to correct. Converting even two or three shots would change his whole efficiency line.

nextGame.watch: His completion rate on throws of 20+ air yards against a secondary without Benford. If the shots start landing, the 0.08 EPA season becomes a blip.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect efficiency to climb back toward his recent standard, though probably not all the way to last year's 0.228. Several things are sustainable: low pressure, quick sack avoidance, aggressive intent, a top-four defense creating leads, and a pass-leaning play-caller. Several things should regress: a 28.6% deep completion rate, a 3.7% interception rate above his recent norm, and five picks bunched into one-score states. The yardage pace near 297 a game, however, was propped up by two 50-plus-attempt games and should settle lower as game scripts improve.

The real risks are his age and how thin the receiving corps is behind Adams. Nacua's quiet start, the tight end injuries and Mumpfield's shoulder all narrow the passing tree. If Adams draws extra coverage and the second option doesn't step up, the short game's empty production will keep sinking third downs.
swingFactors: Whether his deep accuracy recovers or reflects age
A second receiver emerging behind Adams
Pass protection holding near a 14% pressure rate

bets.reason: Buffalo allows 2.5 quarterback touchdowns a game (29th) and ranks 28th in pass EPA, and its top corner is out. His touchdown rate (3.7%, 27th) is well below what his 46-touchdown 2025 suggests he is.

Buffalo gives up 297 yards a game to quarterbacks and ranks 27th in explosive passes allowed, and the game is in a dome. The edge is only slight because his average was built on 55 and 51 attempts. If the Rams lead, volume could fall even as his efficiency rises.

The Rams defense is 4th in EPA and 1st in explosive pass rate and deep EPA allowed, which blunts Buffalo's 3rd-ranked offense. Only one of the Rams' four games has cleared 54 combined points. A mid-pack Rams offense (15th in EPA) is not built for a 30-point night against anyone, though Buffalo's 29th-ranked defense is the main risk to the under.

confidence.note: Four games and 21 deep attempts. The long career baseline argues for regression, but his age adds real doubt.
